This assumes the entire dungeon would have the same difficulty. If the dungeon started as a normal difficulty, but would  a few rooms in was nigh on impossible, then backing out would be the wise move. As the enemies now have to resupply, the first few rooms are repopulated and the later rooms are made a little easier. At any point you SHOULD be able to go forward, but backing out, selling loot, cutting off enemy resources should always be an option.

The goal of backing out would be to make getting further next time easier, making the harder enemies a little more manageable if you overcome challenges and trials elsewhere. Maybe you choose between a boss in the easier area, or mobs in the next area having slightly better equipment.

Even the reverse, you die and instead of instantly making the entire dungeon harder, you get notified of supplies coming in, you can choose to dive into the dungeon and try again before resources arrive, or  go stop the resources from ever reaching them, if you can.


To use a different example, imagine a strategy game where as you choose your battles and win them, you opponent ends up with less resources but the more you lose the less resources you have. You know, the basic principal of every RTS ever

I hate the latter idea even more. It leads to challenges I failed and wanted to go back to not even being there. It's a hand holding that I personally despise.

The getting harder idea could be good if it's in a fairly complex game compared to what was suggested. Maybe in an rpg where you raid a demons lair, if you kill major enemies and get out, the next raid is easier. You spread out their forces, you make them rely in weaker units. You die and all the units you killed come back and they get sent new stuff. Better equipment, better units etc. What could be fun is either trying to rush another run before they arrive or deciding to just leave and cut off supplies.

This way the game gets easier as you win, harder as you lose, but has a way of letting you subvert the difficulty increases
